title: How our town gets to work
scenario: You volunteer for a local transport group. Your colleague Priya is on the phone and can't see the survey chart. She has to decide whether to ask the council for more cycle lanes or more buses. Explain what the data shows so she can decide.

source.caption: How residents usually travel to work (% of people surveyed, 2016 and 2026)

task.audience: a colleague who can't see the chart and has to make a decision
task.prompt: Explain the chart to Priya in about one minute (90–140 words). Give the overall picture first, then the two biggest changes with figures, and say what it might mean for her decision. Don't read out every number.

points.idea: Overall: the car is still the most common way, but much less than before.
Car use fell sharply, from 58% to 41%.
Cycling more than tripled, from 6% to 19%.
Bus use stayed roughly the same (17% → 15%).
What it suggests for the decision (demand is growing for cycling, not buses), with a cautious word.

leave_out.idea: Reading out the walking figures one by one (14% → 13%) – they don't affect the decision.

model: OK, so the chart compares how people got to work in 2016 and 2026. Overall, the car is still the most common way, but it's dropped a lot – from 58% to 41%. The biggest change is cycling: it's more than tripled, from 6% to 19%, so almost one in five people now cycle. Buses, on the other hand, have hardly changed – around 15 to 17%. Walking is about the same too, and more people work from home now. So if you're choosing between the two, the data suggests that demand is growing for cycling rather than buses. More cycle lanes would probably match what people are already doing – though we might want to ask bus users why they aren't switching.
useful: Overall, … is still the most common …, but …
The biggest change is … : it's gone from … to …
tips: Someone who can't see a chart needs the big picture first, then two or three key numbers – not a list of every figure.
Round and compare: "almost one in five", "more than tripled" are easier to follow on the phone than "19 per cent" alone.
End with what the data means for the listener's decision, and hedge it (suggests, probably) – a survey doesn't prove everything.
explain: A strong answer gives the overview (cars still first but falling), the two biggest changes with figures (car 58→41, cycling 6→19), notes that buses barely changed, and links this cautiously to Priya's decision.
